evidence.section_title: Cognitive Bibliotherapy for Mild and Moderate Adolescent Depressive Symptomatology
evidence.quote: [/page/0/Text/7] For several years, we have been exploring the efficacy of self-administered cognitive therapy for depression. The original investigations were with depressed older adult participants involved in what we chose to call cognitive bibliotherapy (Scogin, Hamblin, & Beutler, 1987; Scogin, Jamison, & Gochneaur, 1989). This treatment consisted of reading Feeling Good (Burns 1980), a self-administered version of cognitive therapy for depression, and receiving weekly monitoring telephone calls from a researcher associated with the project.

[/page/1/Text/11] The treatment condition in our study was cognitive bibliotherapy for depression. The book used was Feeling Good (Burns, 1980), which has a theoretical foundation derived from Beck's (1970) cognitive theory of depression.
The intervention described is "bibliotherapy" which is a form of CBT.
[/page/3/Text/4] the process consistent with the cognitive theory of depression.
[/page/3/Text/7] We analyzed scores on the CBT by using a 2 \times 2 (Condition \times Time) repeated measures ANOVA. ... knowledge of the concepts presented in the bibliotherapy treatment
[/page/4/Text/8] The results of our study suggest that cognitive bibliotherapy may be an effective treatment for adolescents experiencing depressive symptoms

evidence.quote: [/page/0/Text/5] The efficacy of cognitive bibliotherapy for adolescents experiencing mild and moderate depressive symptomatology was examined with a group of 22 community-dwelling adolescents. [/page/0/Text/9] The purpose of our study was to investigate the efficacy of cognitive bibliotherapy with adolescents reporting elevated depressive symptoms.

[/page/0/Text/12] Inclusion criteria were a score of 10 or higher on the Child Depression Inventory (CDI; Kovacs, 1981), a score of 10 or higher on the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HRSD; Hamilton, 1960)

[/page/1/Text/9] Potential participants were assessed for eligibility through an initial telephone call. Appropriate participants were then invited for a screening interview and initial assessment. The initial assessment phase consisted of administration of the PIAT-R Reading Comprehension Test, the CDI, the ATQ, the DAS, the CBT, the CBCL, and the HRSD. [/page/1/Text/10] Following this initial assessment, participants meeting inclusion criteria were assigned on a random basis to either the immediate-treatment condition or the delayed-treatment condition.

[/page/1/Text/15] We compared the immediate-treatment and delayed-treatment conditions on age, gender, race, reading comprehension, and initial levels of depressive symptoms to determine if there were any significant differences between the two conditions before treatment.

[/page/4/Text/10] Finally, the presence of depressive symptoms—and not a diagnosis of major depression or dysthymia—was required for entry into our study, so our results should not be generalized to people with major depression or dysthymia.
